articles.title: Ulster Rugby: Robert Baloucoune, James McNabney and Joe Hopes sign contract extensions
articles.summary: Robert Baloucoune, James McNabney and Joe Hopes sign contract extensions with Ulster.
articles.body:
Robert Baloucoune, James McNabney and Joe Hopes have signed contract extensions with Ulster.

Ireland wing Baloucoune has penned fresh terms after a memorable 2026 in which the 29-year-old's eye-catching Six Nations displays earned him the championship's Rising Player award.

Back rower McNabney's new deal comes a week after he was called up to the Ireland squad, with the 23-year-old having made his Ulster return last month following a year out with a serious knee injury.

Versatile forward Hopes, who can play at lock or in the back row, has also committed his future after breaking into the senior team last season.

The 2022 Ulster Schools' player of the year made his debut aged 19 in 2023 and featured off the bench in the Challenge Cup win over Zebre earlier this month.

Ulster said all three have signed new deals until "at least" the summer of 2029.

"We are delighted to have secured the futures of Rob, James and Joe," added general manager Rory Best.

"Rob has showcased his importance to this Ulster team and the national team with his abilities and performances. He is a Test-level winger who has really benefited from a run of games over the past year.

"Both James and Joe are working hard in the early stages of their professional careers and have both shown a lot of potential in our forward pack."

Best added: "Everyone here was delighted to see James called up to the Ireland squad after the adversity he faced coming back from a long-term knee injury.

"We have full belief that all three will form an important part of our Ulster team in the coming years and look forward to seeing what they produce on the field."

images.caption: Image caption, Rob Baloucoune, James McNabney and Joe Hopes have all signed new deals until "at least" the summer of 2029

articles.title: Cheika happy to 'fly the flag' for Lebanon
articles.summary: Lebanon head coach Michael Cheika says he will be approaching the concluding fixture of his side's 2026 Rugby League World Cup campaign as if it is the final...
articles.body:
Having been involved in World Cup, Heineken Cup and Super Rugby finals in rugby union, an apparent dead-rubber fixture to conclude his side's involvement at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup may not initially seem to be among the most significant moments of Michael Cheika's storied coaching career.

However, the 59-year-old Australian says he will be treating Lebanon's meeting with France on Sunday (06:50 GMT) as if it were another final.

The Cedars, who reached the quarter-finals four years ago under Cheika, have been defeated by Papua New Guinea and Tonga in their opening two games, ending any hopes of reaching the knockout stages of this abridged tournament.

"We've got the one game here against France on Sunday and it's really our Grand Final," said the Australian, whose side did not have a fixture between this World Cup and the last.

"I know it'll be for France as well, knowing some players inside of their team.

"I suppose it's not the climax of the tournament, but definitely for us this is a finals fixture and we're approaching it that way."

Born to Lebanese migrants, Cheika believes the relative rarity of being able to represent the country on a world stage means every opportunity to do so is special.

"The people in Lebanon are watching. I know my own relatives, they're watching and how often do they get to support their national teams on the world stage? How often do you get to support the flag?

"Compare it to Aussies, we're getting to support a national team every five minutes, right?

"For the Lebanese, it's not that simple and I just think the ability to let people see that their team is playing on the world stage is a buzz."

Cheika's involvement with the team and the sport carries special personal significance too, providing a link back to the country of his ancestors that his family left in 1950 in search of a "better life".

"It's a game that somehow has built a connection with the country from a distance," he said of Lebanon's interest in rugby league.

"I can tell a story of my own dad when he arrived, he didn't know where to go, he didn't have any connections or anything, so they dropped him in Redfern which is where the local Lebanese church is.

"Across the road from there is the Redfern Oval where South Sydney played. To integrate into the local community, to become Aussies, he thought let's go to the footy. Never seen it before, but started going over. That very working class Lebanese migrant that came here, they really connected to the game of rugby league.

"And I think now for the boys to be able to represent their heritage in their area of expertise, their passion, that's something I never thought I could do. I thought the only way I could help would be to do something for charity or politics but here we have an opportunity to fly the flag for people."

While Cheika grew up watching both rugby codes, he concedes that there are challenges to swapping back and forth between the two.

His last role in the 15-a-side game was with Leicester Tigers for the 2024-25 season and he will return to the Waratahs, where he won a title in 2014, for next year's Super Rugby campaign.

Fluent in Arabic, French and Italian, he likens the process to moving between languages.

"You find out there's different grammar, different sentence construction. There's different emphasis on words or different accents, but at the end of the day, the values of what the player needs to have, those things are the same.

"Courage, aggression, commitment, the trust in your team-mates, all those types of things are the same."

While work has already begun in the background for his Waratahs return, he does not believe Sunday's game will be his last in League.

"It's been unreal, I've got to admit," he added.

"Last year, I think, was my 27th year coaching and it was something so fresh.

"I feel like I'll cross back and forth a few more times yet, hopefully, before no one wants to know about me any longer."
authors: Jonathan Bradley - BBC Sport NI senior journalist

articles.title: Bristol Bears: Saracens did everything they could before sacking Totoa Auvaa
articles.summary: Bristol Bears director of rugby Pat Lam tells BBC Radio Bristol Saracens did everything they could for Totoa Auvaa before he was sacked by them.
articles.body:
Saracens did everything they could for Samoan forward Totoa Auvaa before sacking him, according to his new director of rugby at Bristol Bears.

Auvaa, 21, was involved in a nightclub altercation with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson in June, though Sarries stood by him at the time.

He was, however, sacked two weeks ago following another late-night incident in St Albans, which police are investigating.

When Auvaa's signing was announced on Monday , Bristol boss Pat Lam said he believed in giving people second chances.

On Wednesday he told BBC Radio Bristol: "People make mistakes. I felt he will fit in well here.

"He's training this week and looks very impressive. There's no doubt that we believe he's someone that has ability to grow and develop as a really outstanding rugby player."

Lam revealed that England, British & Irish Lions and Saracens captain Maro Itoje had checked in on Auvaa this week as he started life with the Bears.

Lam said: "Saracens did an unbelievable job, they gave him the opportunity, they got him an English teacher, Maro itoje has been like a mentor to him.

"Maro got hold of him yesterday to check in and see how he's doing. They did as well as they could, the decision they made they felt was right and I understand that.

"I was asked if I would give him another opportunity and I am happy to do it."

Lam hopes he can be a positive influence on his fellow Samoan and said Auvaa had not been issued with any ultimatums about his future behaviour.

He said: "We highlight what we expect. Every player has some sort of past but the past is in the past and you have got to learn.

"My whole thing in life, with five kids at nearly 60, I look back and go, there were lots of ups and downs, but I am who I am because of the experiences I went through and then having the right people.

"Some of the decisions I made, rugby influenced a lot of it and people who mentored me and took me under their wing shaped me this way.

"I have benefited from it. There's a lot of stories that could go this way or the other way. The beauty of our great game is every good team has a good environment.

"We're all human, there's no guarantees, you're always going to be criticised for anything and praised for different things, you just have to keep pushing through.

"This is human nature. It depends who's giving you the opportunity. I see him no different to lots of people on this earth that have made mistakes."

Auvaa made one senior appearance for Saracens, playing 20 minutes of a Prem Rugby Cup match in September.

But Lam hinted that he might match that number for Bears very soon with two group games to come in the competition against Sale and Bath in November.

Lam added: "He'll look to feature in the Prem Cup. He's got to learn all of our systems and our ways. He's made a good start. It's about how quickly you can learn."

images.caption: Image caption, Forward Auvaa has been signed by Bristol after being let go by Saracens this month

articles.title: PREM Rugby and RFU committed to expanding top flight with English clubs despite Welsh interest
articles.summary: PREM Rugby and RFU say they are committed to English clubs being in the expansion of the top flight; a report said Welsh Rugby Union is in advanced discussions with PREM Rugby and the RFU over the possibility of turning it into a cross-border competition
articles.body:
Reports emerged on Wednesday that suggested the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) was interested in joining a cross-border competition.

The PREM is aiming expand from 10 to 12 sides in time for the 2029/2030 season but PREM Rugby and the Rugby Football Union (RFU) insist their priority is to back domestic teams.

"Resources are currently focused on supporting English clubs throughout the pyramid who aspire to join the league," they said in a joint statement.

"The PREM is an attractive league and responsibility for its expansion sits with the Men's Professional Rugby Board (MPRB), which has established detailed entry criteria that any prospective club would need to satisfy."

Despite that position, the WRU - which last week announced a loss of £18.1m for 2025/26 - issued a statement confirming its commitment to supplying four teams to the United Rugby Championship until the 2027/28 season while also highlighting the attraction of joining the Prem.

"By the end of the 2027/28 season, the WRU will have determined the future operating model for the men's game in Wales," the statement read.

"The WRU will continue to work with other shareholders in the URC on future Welsh representation in the competition.

"The WRU keeps under review the competition opportunities which may be available across the game and could be in the best interests of Welsh rugby.

"The idea of Anglo-Welsh competitions is something that is often debated by Welsh rugby fans.

"The WRU understands the appeal of the English top-flight, which is why we are pitching for two of our women's teams, Brython Thunder and Gwalia Lightning, to be included in Premiership Women's Rugby."

images.caption: Image: The RFU says it is committed to the expansion of the top flight involving English clubs

articles.title: Anglo-Welsh league: Prem Rugby cool on idea despite WRU interest
articles.summary: Welsh rugby may be keen on forming an Anglo-Welsh league but the Prem and RFU are only looking at English clubs in any expansion.
articles.body:
English rugby bosses have confirmed they are concentrating on expanding the Prem with English clubs rather than bringing in teams from Wales.

Prem Rugby, which runs the English top flight, has released a joint statement alongside the Rugby Football Union (RFU) stating they were looking at adding two English clubs by 2029.

This came after reports the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has expressed an interest in joining an Anglo-Welsh league.

The Professional Rugby Board (PRB), which runs the professional game in Wales, met on Wednesday and were told the WRU plans to explore a future in the English club game.

While senior sources in English club rugby have confirmed interest from the WRU, they insist negotiations are not taking place.

The Prem has been reduced to 10 sides after Wasps, Worcester and London Irish were forced to fold during the 2022-23 season.

Traditional promotion and relegation to and from the top tier has been scrapped from the start of the 2026-27 season after landmark changes to English rugby were voted through.

Instead of earning a play-off shot at replacing the Prem's bottom side by finishing top of the second-tier Champ and meeting the top flight's minimum standards, clubs will instead apply to join and be judged across a range of criteria.

Bids will be assessed on standard of play, finances, investment potential, infrastructure and how their geographical base could help spread the Prem's appeal, among other factors.

The league hopes to initially expand to 12 teams for the 2029-30 season with a "long-term ambition" to grow further.

Conditions were initially set that any team wanting to play in the Prem will need to complete a campaign in the Champ before being considered.

A joint Prem Rugby and RFU statement said: "Prem Rugby and the RFU are committed to expanding the English top-flight, with a provisional target season to grow to 12 teams by 2029-30.

"The Prem is an attractive league and responsibility for its expansion sits with the Men's Professional Rugby Board (MPRB), which has established detailed entry criteria that any prospective club would need to satisfy.

"Resources are currently focused on supporting English clubs throughout the pyramid who aspire to join the league."

The RFU would have to approve Welsh teams moving into the league due to it becoming a cross-border competition.

Wales have four professional sides, Ospreys, Cardiff, Scarlets and Dragons, that currently play in the 16-team United Rugby Championship (URC) which includes teams from Scotland, Ireland, Italy and South Africa.

Welsh rugby's governing body, along with the other national unions, are stakeholders in that league.

While English bosses have revealed their intentions were on welcoming English clubs, the WRU released a more non-committal statement where they did not rule out continuing the English interest.

"Welsh men's professional teams compete in the URC and the WRU is committed to providing four teams to the URC until the end of the 2027-28 season," it read.

"By the end of this season, the WRU will have determined the future operating model for the men's game in Wales.

"The WRU will continue to work with other shareholders in the URC on future Welsh representation in the competition.

"The WRU keeps under review the competition opportunities which may be available across the game and could be in the best interests of Welsh rugby.

"The idea of Anglo-Welsh competitions is something often debated by Welsh rugby fans.

"The WRU understands the appeal of the English top-flight, which is why we are pitching for two of our women's teams, Brython Thunder and Gwalia Lightning, to be included in Premiership Women's Rugby."

The WRU posted an £18m loss for the latest financial year - compared to a £7.2m loss the previous year.

The union says it is already predicting a similar loss next year, and say the figures back up its case that four professional regions are no longer sustainable.

WRU chief financial officer Gavin Marshall said they could only spend £20m on professional rugby, compared to the £26m it contributes now.

However it is understood the Prem "P-share" - effectively the up-front cost to enter the league - is valued at £20m.

The "P-share" secures a percentage of central income and voting rights and the requirement to fund a Premiership Women's Rugby programme.

How any new Anglo-Welsh tournament ties in with WRU plans to cut a professional side by 2028 remains to be seen.

The governing body has stated it will press ahead with these plans with three licences awarded, one in the capital, one in the east and one in the west.

Ospreys and Scarlets are set to fight to be the side in west Wales, with Cardiff, currently owned by the WRU, and Dragons - an independently-backed business - safe under current proposals.

As it stands, a rugby summit has been called for December with a final decision expected on which club will be culled to be made in the summer of 2027.

But Faulkner has also promised to review the three-team proposal as the uncertainty in Welsh rugby remains.

articles.title: Red Roses: Ellie Kildunne named on bench for second England match in a row
articles.summary: Red Roses' star Ellie Kildunne is named on England's bench again as head coach John Mitchell makes six changes to his side to face the United States.
articles.body:
Ellie Kildunne has been named on the England bench for their fixture against the USA, despite head coach John Mitchell making six changes to his side.

The 27-year-old full-back was dropped for the 31-22 defeat by Canada last Saturday, with Mitchell saying she needed to show "greater consistency".

Despite the loss in Ottawa, Bristol Bears star Kildunne will once again have to settle for a place on the bench for Friday's match against the USA in New Jersey, with Emma Sing retaining her spot.

With 67 England caps to her name, Kildunne was named World Rugby's player of the year in 2024, and starred in the Red Roses' 2025 World Cup victory.

Four of Mitchell's changes are to the backs, with Tatyana Heard, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Flo Robinson and Holly Aitchison handed their first starts of the tour, while forwards Mackenzie Carson and Maud Muir replace Hannah Botterman and Sarah Bern.

"Our intent is to start this next phase strongly against the USA, with six months until our next Test in the Women's Six Nations," said Mitchell.

"We're rotating some positions this week to refresh the group, create opportunities and continue building our depth.

"Selection is driven by what the team needs against the USA, the behaviours we value and the performance we're preparing to deliver.

"Everyone has a role, and everyone is accountable for our standards."

England: Sing; Venner, Jones, Heard, Moloney-MacDonald; Aitchison, Robinson; Carson, Cokayne, Muir, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Kabeya, Feaunati

Replacements: Field, Botterman, Bern, Short, Matthews, Hunt, Harrison, Kildunne

images.caption: Image caption, Ellie Kildunne scored two tries and two assists in the last meeting with the USA in August 2025

articles.title: WXV Global Series: England make six changes for United States match but Ellie Kildunne remains on bench
articles.summary: England have made six changes for their final WXV Global Series match against the USA on Friday (kick-off 9.15pm GMT); Ellie Kildunne remains on the bench; Red Roses go into match after back-to-back losses to Canada
articles.body:
The Red Roses were beaten in back-to-back games for the first time in a decade when their 41-Test unbeaten run came to an end against Canada, who were then triumphant again a week later.

Head coach John Mitchell has reacted to the result in Ottawa by making extensive changes for Friday's match, including a first start for scrum-half Flo Robinson.

Having featured in both Canada games at fly-half, Zoe Harrison is demoted to the bench with Holly Aitchison taking over as chief playmaker and there are returns for wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and centre Tatyana Heard.

The promotion of Mackenzie Carson and Maud Muir to the front row completes the changes, with Ellie Kildunne remaining on the bench.

"Our intent is to start this next phase strongly against the USA, with six months until our next Test in the Six Nations," Mitchell said.

"We're rotating some positions this week to refresh the group, create opportunities and continue building our depth.

"Selection is driven by what the team needs against the USA, the behaviours we value and the performance we're preparing to deliver.

"Everyone has a role, and everyone is accountable for our standards."

England: 15 Emma Sing, 14 Mia Venner, Meg Jones (c), 12 Tatyana Heard, 11 Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, 10 Holly Aitchison, 9 Flo Robinson; 1 Mackenzie Carson, 2 Amy Cokayne, 3 Maud Muir; 4 Morwenna Talling, 5 Lilli Ives Campion; 6 Abi Burton, 7 Sadia Kabeya, 8 Maddie Feaunati.

Replacements: 16 Bryony Field, 17 Hannah Botterman, 18 Sarah Bern, 19 Demelza Short, 20 Alex Matthews; 21 Natasha Hunt, 22 Zoe Harrison, 23 Ellie Kildunne.

images.caption: Image: Ellie Kildunne remains on the bench for the Red Roses

articles.title: 17-0! Indian rugby girls steal the show against New Zealand side
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Even as the Abhishek Sharma blitzkrieg dominated headlines in the morning, there was a different India-New Zealand sporting chatter that
articles.body: KOLKATA: Even as the Abhishek Sharma blitzkrieg dominated headlines in the morning, there was a different India-New Zealand sporting chatter that dominated social media in the evening.It was the video of one of the two successful tries by the Indian U20 women’s rugby sevens team against a team from heavyweights New Zealand comprising U20 Maori players from the country at Rajgir International Sports Complex on Tuesday.The match was a part of the India-New Zealand U20 Rugby Series as part of the 100 Years of Unity through Sport initiative.And while the Indian girls’ spectacular performance was against an invitational team from New Zealand, a 17-0 shut-out win over any All Blacks team deserves the attention the historic victory got around the country.The Indian squad put on a masterclass in structural discipline and tackle precision, storming to a 12–0 half-time lead before sealing the huge shutout with a final late try.“It was a once in a lifetime experience! I had only watched videos of the New Zealand teams’ matches before. It was great to be able to play with them,” India U20 player Akshaya NS said after the match as she shared a hug with her counterpart from New Zealand, Anyis Drossaerts Lake.While the team’s feat grabbed eyeballs on Tuesday, it was not the first achievement of an Indian women’s rugby team with the senior women’s national team attaining their best-ever Asian Games finish of sixth in Nagoya earlier this month. The Asiad campaign this time, that saw a lot of improvement from their show in Hangzhou 2022, was also the first time that an Indian women’s team had won two of its group games.There has been a steady development in Indian rugby since former South Africa rugby player moved to India in 2022, initially to work with Bihar Rugby, and has now been a member of the coaching staff and high-performance coach and scout for Rugby India.The U20 Rugby series under the 100 years’ initiative featured joint training sessions, cultural interactions and four Rugby Sevens matches, including, for the first time, two mixed-team matches in which players from India and New Zealand played together.“The mixed match was really fun as we got to play together after playing against one another,” Akshaya said pointing to Lake.“But one of the best experiences was watching a live Haka here in Rajgir in front of our very eyes,” added the excited Indian youngster.The New Zealand U20 Maori men’s team, before beating the Indian U20 men 32-0, gave everyone a taste of their culture with a Haka performance before the kick-off.The series emphasised the role of sport in advancing bilateral ties, cultural understanding and youth development, reflecting sport’s increasing importance in India’s international engagement and fostering a more connected global sporting community.It also built on an ongoing cooperation between Rugby India and New Zealand Rugby and in May this year, New Zealand Rugby coaching educators conducted a development programme for 35 Indian coaches at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar, aiming to enhance coaching capabilities and support rugby’s growth in India.As Rugby India chairman Rahul Bose put it, “The India-New Zealand U20 Rugby Series is about much more than the game itself. As we mark 100 years of sporting ties between our countries, bringing these young players together reflects the values that make rugby special: respect, teamwork and friendship.”Pic credit: Rugby IndiaGet the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: How England must harness their underdog spirit to reach the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals
articles.summary: England women face Samoa in their winner-takes-all final group game on Friday (6.45am kick-off); England men face Papua New Guinea in their final Rugby League World Cup pool fixture also on Friday (9.05am kick-off)
articles.body:
They trail Samoa by 68 points on points difference and cannot finish above Tonga because of their head-to-head record, leaving their hopes of progressing dependent on a convincing win and results elsewhere going their way.

That means they must beat Papua New Guinea by as big a margin as possible, then hope Tonga defeat Samoa by enough to give England a route into the semi-finals.

If that all aligns, into the semi-finals they will go.

England's women, meanwhile, face a more straightforward equation. A win against Samoa would secure their place in the semi-finals, but it would rank among the biggest victories of their campaign. They are capable of pulling it off, but the challenge is clear.

England were beaten 78-0 by the Jillaroos, while Samoa lost 40-0 to the same opposition. Those results offer a stark indication of the task ahead.

Both England sides need to show the fighting spirit that has become synonymous with the nation as they look to make their mark on the other side of the world.

England's men may sit third in the international rankings, but that is not how they are viewed Down Under. Australia, New Zealand, Tonga and Samoa are all considered ahead of them, despite England having whitewashed both Tonga and Samoa in recent series.

The complicated group structure has done Brian McDermott's side few favours. They effectively had one chance to put themselves in a strong position, and they needed to beat Tonga in their opening match to do so. Instead, they lost 30-12.

Even two wins from their remaining games - and convincing ones at that - may not be enough to save their campaign.

They could be enough despite England's men not meeting up once before the tournament. They could be enough despite having just two training sessions to prepare for their opening group match. They could be enough with the odds stacked against them.

Both England teams face an uphill battle, albeit for different reasons. While the men must overcome a difficult qualification equation, the women face opponents with greater experience of playing together.

Samoa's women, in particular, boast a squad packed with young, emerging talent who play week in, week out in the National Rugby League Women's Premiership (NRLW), gaining regular experience in one of the world's most intense women's rugby league competitions.

They were viewed before the tournament as the team most capable of pushing the Jillaroos closest. But England should not be written off after their heavy opening defeat. The 2022 Rugby League World Cup offers a reminder of why: England's men demolished Samoa in their opening game, only to be beaten by them in the semi-finals.

For England's women, the equation is simpler: beat Samoa and reach the semi-finals. With their place in the last four on the line, they must show that, despite the women's game in England still being a work in progress, they can compete with the best on the international stage.

There has been plenty of discussion about what international rugby league needs to thrive: greater investment, more mid-season internationals and more opportunities for the global game to capture the public's attention. The need for that backing is clear.

The prospect of both England sides exiting at the group stage has been described as a potential wake-up call for the sport in this hemisphere - a chance to invest in players, give the international game greater prominence and find a way to close the gap on the other side of the world.

But this is not a new conversation. After England's men fell short at the 2008 World Cup, figures at the top of the sport reviewed what had gone wrong. Many remain influential today, underlining how long these questions have persisted.

Failure can force change. But perhaps the bigger shock - and the more powerful catalyst - would be for England to succeed when so few expect them to.

If the men and women both defy the odds and reach the semi-finals, it would be more than a sporting triumph. It would be a statement that English rugby league can compete, and an opportunity to build momentum for the international game rather than wait for another failure to force the issue.

McDermott said before the tournament that a visit to just one NRL club would show how remarkable it is that England can compete, given the infrastructure available Down Under. The playing field is so uneven that England's position among the international elite is an achievement in itself.

Too often, we judge England's rugby league teams by how far they still have to go. But is it time to look instead at how much they have achieved in spite of the disadvantages they face?

Could that be the catalyst for people to recognise the potential of English rugby league and give it the backing it deserves?

The sport has long searched for its lightbulb moment: the spark that sets change in motion, the first domino to fall. Perhaps, rather than another setback being needed to force that change, this could be the tournament in which success provides the catalyst.

It remains a long shot. England know the task ahead is monumental, but they persist regardless.

They will take that fight into their clashes with Papua New Guinea and Samoa, and by Sunday we will know how far their persistence has taken them.

For England, it is not about the resources they lack, but the fight they show and what they can achieve against the odds.

articles.title: James McNabney: Horses, farming and ACL injury - Ulster back row's rise
articles.summary: Ulster back row James McNabney speaks about horse riding, his ACL injury and his dad's reaction to his first Ireland call-up.
articles.body:
"Will you ever be home to the farm again?"

That was the light-hearted response from James McNabney's father after he was called into the Ireland squad for the first time.

When the news came, the 23-year-old back row was in South Africa with Ulster and, without an eSIM in his phone, was trying to connect to WiFi when out for coffee.

When finally online, he saw the email that said he had earned an Ireland call-up from Andy Farrell.

"I was delighted. It was a big moment for the family as well," McNabney said.

"My mum was very proud and I don't think my dad knew what way to take it at the start.

"But no, they're both delighted for me and I appreciate the support they've given me."

McNabney keen to show Ireland coaches 'what I'm all about'

Ringrose set to miss Ireland's November games

McNabney's route into the Ireland set-up is not the traditional path taken by most players.

Growing up on a farm in Ballymena, he did not watch a lot of rugby growing up and only started playing in school. At the time, horses were his focus.

Long before he had even dreamt of becoming a professional rugby player, he had represented Northern Ireland and Great Britain's equestrian teams.

"I rode horses from when I was about six until I was 16," he said.

"Horses was sort of a main hobby, then it became a sport for me."

At 16 he was given an ultimatum over his sporting future.

"Michael Black [a provincial talent coach] from Ulster was like, 'you need to make the decision whether you're going to put on a bit of timber and play rugby or stay lean and ride a horse'.

"I decided to play rugby. I was enjoying it, I stuck at it and here I am."

As for equestrian, there's no more horsing around for the big back row.

"We've still got one at home. If I'm taken to the field then I'll maybe jump on it.

"Other than that, I only do it for the craic. I haven't been on a horse in, I'd say, six months."

Given his other interests, McNabney says he did not have a lot of rugby heroes growing up and instead simply "enjoyed playing it".

"I didn't really watch it that much. That probably went against me because I was quite green, and didn't know much about it.

"But it wasn't until I was getting to Ireland Under-20s that I really thought this is what I'm going to do for a job."

An Under-20 Six Nations Grand Slam winner in 2022 and 2023, McNabney's senior Ireland chance came more than a year later than he initially hoped.

After an impressive season with Ulster, he had been included by Farrell as a training panellist for the 2025 Six Nations.

He was set to be included again for the summer fixtures against Japan and Georgia when the bulk of the front-liners were away with the British and Irish Lions, but he did not get to meet up with the squad after he sustained an ACL injury.

He only returned to action for Ulster in pre-season this summer after a year on the sidelines, and the fact Farrell has included him in the Ireland panel again at the first time of asking shows how highly he is rated by the coaching group.

At 6ft 5in and almost 19 stone, it's easy to see why Farrell described him as "some specimen of a man".

McNabney said it was the worst injury you can get as a player, but that "you just have to be patient".

"I tried to set a goalpost of where I wanted to be to get back. And then different things happened. I learned to just take it a day at a time.

"Each player is different and their bodies react differently to everything. So I just had to learn that there are going to be setbacks.

"We've got it here now and I'm delighted that I pushed through."

'I don't have the expectation of being capped'

Now in a position to impress Farrell and his coaching team, McNabney could make his Ireland debut in November's Nations Championship matches against Argentina, Fiji, South Africa or during the finals weekend in London at the end of the month.

He says he is "delighted" he has got a chance, but even if he doesn't get any minutes on the pitch he is more than happy to play a role this autumn.

When asked what his goal was for the camp, he said to "learn as much as possible and hopefully earn my first cap".

"I don't have the expectation that I'm going to get capped. I'm here to work hard, show what I'm about.

"Just because I'm picked in the squad doesn't mean I'm necessarily going to play.

"Hopefully I train hard, get picked, and hopefully Faz [Farrell] sees what I see in myself and backs me.

"I'll just work hard and prepare the team as best as I can for the games coming up."

Given his laid-back demeanour, it's no surprise to hear that McNabney "hasn't been too fixed" on whether he will or will not make his Ireland bow in the next five weeks.

"Every young player wants to play for Ireland someday. It's hard to get into the team, that doesn't just happen," he added.

"Someday I might wear the green, but I still haven't worn it yet."

Image caption, James McNabney won the Under-20 Six Nations Grand Slam with Ireland in 2022 and 2023

articles.title: Wales' Sean Lynn makes five changes for WXV rematch against Japan
articles.summary: Head coach Sean Lynn makes five changes for Saturday's WXV Test against Japan following last week's impressive second-half performance.
articles.body:
Wales have made five starting changes for Saturday's second WXV Test against Japan.

Flanker Bethan Lewis will make her first start of the campaign, having been one of Wales' impressive impact players in last weekend's 17-0 victory in Tokyo, with co-captain Alex Callender moving to number eight.

Gwen Crabb and Gwenllian Pyrs are also promoted from the bench to join the pack, while Lleucu George is preferred to Keira Bevan at fly-half.

George will partner Seren Lockwood, who crossed for two tries last weekend, as Wales seek back-to-back wins (07:00 GMT).

Courtney Keight comes in for centre Freya Bell, who looks set for a lengthy lay-off after suffering a serious knee injury in the opening Test.

Head coach Sean Lynn has again opted for six forwards and two backs on the bench.

"We have made the changes to reward the players who finished the job in Tokyo," said Lynn.

Wales are looking to finish their WXV campaign on a high at Kumagaya Rugby Stadium, having previously beaten Japan and South Africa and narrowly lost to USA.

They are ranked 11th in the world after overtaking Saturday's opponents with last week's victory.

Kumagaya Rugby Stadium, Saitama Prefecture

Live on iplayer and BBC Sport website & app. Audio commentary on Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra & BBC Radio Cymru.

"The players know our DNA is 'team first'. Competition for places drives standards and performances and will only help us improve and get better as a team," Lynn added.

"We are obviously disappointed with the injury to Freya Bell, but she will get the best care and we hope to see her back soon."

While last weekend was another welcome win for Lynn, Wales made hard work of the victory in testing conditions.

"We found a way in the first Test in Tokyo and the way the players problem-solved during the game was key for all the coaches," said Lynn.

"But we know we have to be much more accurate and produce a consistent, 80-minute performance to beat a resilient Japan side that we know will be hurting."

Wales: Neumann; N Metcalfe, Cox, Keight, A Williams; George, Lockwood, Pyrs, K Jones, Tuipulotu, B Metcalfe, Crabb, K Williams (co-capt), Lewis, Callender (co-capt).

Replacements: Reardon, Davies, E Jones, Aiono, Evans, King, Bevan, De Vera.

Assistants: Sunny Lee (HKCR), Hibiki Ikeda (JRFU)

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Be patient - England's blueprint for semi-final bid
articles.summary: England boss Brian McDermott has urged his players not to panic as they chase points against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday in a bid to keep alive their Rugby League World Cup hopes.
articles.body:
England boss Brian McDermott has urged his players not to panic as they chase points against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday (09:05 GMT) in a bid to keep alive their Rugby League World Cup hopes.

For the second successive week, England will have an eye on the scoreboard as they aim to claim a handsome win over the Kumuls.

England need two things to go their way to avoid missing out on the World Cup's last four for the first time ever. They require a points difference swing of 68 on rivals Samoa - who they need to lose to Tonga on Sunday.

And McDermott is keen for his side to stick to the blueprint that helped them thrash France 82-0 last weekend to keep slim prospects of a semi-final berth within their sights.

"I suppose [it's a case of] whatever timescale it is before the arm wrestles starts to open up the game for each team... I'm not sure, it could be 15 [minutes], it could be 20, it could be 35, it could be the first half," McDermott said.

"There's a discipline in that we don't start looking for things or searching for things outside of how we want to play. And that was a really impressive trick against France because we knew we had points in us and they weren't coming for that first 20."

England were scoreless for the first 22 minutes against Laurent Frayssinous' side but went through the gears in the second period to record their biggest-ever margin of victory over France.

In contrast, Papua New Guinea looked well in the contest at the halfway stage of their second group match against Samoa last Saturday - only trailing 14-6 - before imploding in the second period and eventually falling to a 64-6 defeat.

68-point swing and a Tonga win - how England avoid World Cup exit

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

England's pursuit of points has led to Warrington winger Matty Ashton retaining his spot on the left.

And the more offensive style of Hull KR's Jez Litten has been preferred at hooker to Wigan's Brad O'Neill, who was recently crowned Super League Man of Steel and is among the interchanges along with club team-mate Zach Eckersley.

"It's that hard call knowing that you've got to have a tough chat with someone like Brad O'Neill, who's probably not doing anything wrong," McDermott said.

"It's more about, I guess, the best fit for gameplan. They all understand the concept of it being a squad effort. It's not just a team effort.

"We've got a specific task this weekend against PNG and I think it'll be a stiffer test than it was against France last week. And we find ourselves in a similar situation, because we don't just need to beat them, we need to beat them convincingly.

"Picking a team that's best suited to that is the main task. So yeah, they're not the easiest conversations to have, but they are when the player themselves has got a lot of humility - and Brad was great."

While Brisbane Broncos prop Ben Talty is yet to feature for England, late call-up Kallum Watkins is another on the interchange bench with Victor Radley and Jack Welsby dropping out.

Morgan Knowles, meanwhile, is set to appear for the first time in the tournament.

Knowles' physical presence was sorely missed in England's 30-12 defeat by Tonga on 17 October as he recovered from a calf issue.

The Dolphins forward's return to action comes at a busy time - as he and his wife have just welcomed their third child to their family.

"The baby was delivered yesterday [Wednesday]. I haven't spoke to Morgan yet, but he's probably got his hands full changing nappies," McDermott said.

"He's had a fair bit going on, but I'm really keen to get him in the team and looking forward to watching him play tomorrow.

"He'll be good and he's really keen to get back with the team and start playing. Everybody's pleased for Morgan and you know, we'll all go for it."

'I earned my spot' - Lewis can be England hero after controversial selection

England battle hardened for make-or-break Samoa match

Meanwhile, England women's prop Vicky Whitfield has suggested that their chastening 78-0 defeat against reigning world champions Australia was the "best preparation" they could have for a make-or-break final group game against Samoa on Friday (06:45 GMT).

Whoever triumphs in the Pool A contest will earn a spot in the semi-finals against the winners of Pool B, New Zealand.

Whitfield says that England should now be more battle hardened against a Samoa side, who were not as comprehensively outclassed in their 40-0 loss to the Jillaroos in their opener on 16 October.

"It gets us used to that quicker pace. Australia threw a lot of shape at us. So defensively, it was a great test for us to have going into this game," Whitfield said.

"It got us used to mapping off and being able to defend against that sort of shape. So yeah, [it's the] best preparation really.

"We knew coming into this week that this game was the one that was really important to us. We did what we did and then have had that focus of going again and resetting."

While England are yet to appear in a women's final (Great Britain lost to New Zealand in the showpiece match in 2000), a fifth consecutive appearance in the last four has been a clear objective for Stuart Barrow's squad from the outset.

"It's everything that we want," Whitefield said.

"If that was to happen, we would be buzzing as a team and it would just be a really great feeling to know that we've managed to do what we've come out here to do, get to a semi and then hopefully perform in that as well."

images.caption: Image caption, England have never previously failed to reach the knockout stages of the World Cup

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England's Brian McDermott admits side face 'unique task' to progress and can't get distracted
articles.summary: England head coach Brian McDermott speaks to the media on Thursday, as his side seek to avoid historic Rugby League World Cup pool stage exit; England face Papua New Guinea in their final pool fixture on Friday (9.05am kick-off), knowing they need a big win to keep semi-final hopes alive
articles.body:
England are up against it in their bid to make it through to the semi-finals after they lost 30-12 to Tonga in their opening game.

They must beat Papua New Guinea in their final pool game in Woollongong on Friday and then wait until Sunday, when they need Tonga to beat Samoa, upon whom England must also make up a 68-point deficit.

That means tries will be the order of the day against Papua New Guinea but McDermott, who saw his side beat France 82-0 in their second game , has called for patience.

"We've got a specific task this weekend. I think it'll be a stiffer test than it was against France," McDermott said at his Thursday press conference.

"We once again find ourselves in another similar situation, very unique as well, that we don't just need to beat them, we need to be beat them convincingly.

"If we're going to go through, we need to score the points, but we can't get to the points first.

"We've got to get to the physicality first and we're going to manage a very physical team, a very dominant team.

"There's a discipline in that we don't start looking for things or searching for things outside of how we want to play.

"That was really impressive against France because we knew we had points in us and they weren't coming in that first 20 [minutes]. We didn't try to do anything different.

"Every team, and I've been involved in so many teams, where you're winning by a large margin and you either take your foot off the gas because we think it's job done or you start to overplay.

"But against France we stuck to the game model and just put it on rinse and repeat."

While England made hay against the French in Perth, McDermott knows Papua New Guinea represent a tougher task.

"They're well coached by Jason Demetriou, who's got a chunk of players who are playing in the British game as well," he said.

"So I think they are going to be really well co-ordinated."

What do England need to avoid historic early World Cup exit?

Quite simply, before Tonga face Samoa, England must beat Papua New Guinea and do it by a considerable margin.

Samoa's thumping 78-4 win over France in their tournament opener and a 64-6 victory over Papua New Guinea on Saturday leaves them with an impressive +132 point difference.

England beating France takes them to a +64 points difference, 68 points behind Samoa heading into the final round of fixtures. Another win Friday would lift them to four points and level with both Samoa and Tonga.

McDermott's side would then be left to wait 48 hours for the outcome of Tonga vs Samoa in Sydney. A Samoa win would guarantee England's elimination, while a Tonga victory would see the points difference decide second spot.

England don't necessarily need to beat Papua New Guinea by 68 points or more, but a victory by that margin would mean any loss for Samoa would be enough to progress.

A smaller England win would see them need Samoa to lose by a bigger score, depending on England's final points difference.

The winner of the combined Groups B+C table would progress to the semi-finals to face the runner-up of Group A, a four-team league consisting of Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands.

images.caption: Image: England head coach Brian McDermott spoke to media on Thursday as his side seek to avoid a historic first World Cup pool-stage exit
Image: McDermott has previously branded the Rugby League World Cup format 'harsh,' with his side up against it to progress
Image: England were thrashed by Tonga in their opening game at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup

articles.title: Ospreys v Cardiff: Wales wing Josh Adams released for URC derby
articles.summary: Wales wing Josh Adams is set for game time with Cardiff at Ospreys before the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
Wales wing Josh Adams has been released from international camp to start for Cardiff against Ospreys at St Helen's on Saturday in the United Rugby Championship (URC).

The 31-year-old is the only Welsh region-based member of Steve Tandy's squad to be sent out for game time prior to the Nations Championship.

Adams returned from a hamstring injury off the bench at Northampton a fortnight ago and started the defeat by Sharks at Cardiff Arms Park last weekend.

Cardiff head coach Corniel van Zyl said: "Josh has only played close to 100 minutes and if you are to look at Test match preparation you probably need almost double that, so it makes sense."

The Blue and Blacks are without their six other members of the Wales squad and Ospreys are missing four players.

Prem eyes English expansion despite Welsh interest

Wales deputy helps Ospreys make themselves at home

Cardiff are without loose-head prop Rhys Barratt, hooker Liam Belcher, lock Teddy Williams and back-row forwards Alex Mann, James Botham and Taine Basham.

"I would say that you want to see derbies with full squads and both teams being able to select whoever they want," said Van Zyl.

"It's in the schedule, and unfortunately there are priorities with Wales. We lose a few and they lose a few, which will test the squads and lead to opportunities."

Full-back Tom Rogers, fly-half Dan Edwards, scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams and loose-head prop Gareth Thomas sit out the derby for Ospreys, who enjoyed a winning return to St Helen's against Dragons last weekend.

"It is disappointing for the supporters in general," said head coach Mark Jones.

"We are trying to grow the game in Wales, make it front and centre and have as many people in the ground as possible watching.

"That creates a better atmosphere but, from a financial perspective, people spending money want to watch the best players, and that is the challenge.

"That is out of my control and the agreement the regions have with the WRU.

"We have to get on with the cards we have been dealt, and the boys who have been with us have great and get an opportunity.

"But I would have loved to have everybody available and it would be a much better spectacle for the Welsh public."

'I'm no yes-man' - new WRU chair to review region cut

Where are Wales internationals really made?

Lock Josh McNally is the sole survivor in Cardiff's starting pack from the Sharks game and captains the side in the absence of hooker Belcher.

Without Wales back-rowers Mann, Botham and Basham, number eight Alun Lawrence makes a timely return from injury for a first appearance of the season.

In addition to the six Wales internationals who are unavailable, the Blue and Blacks are without 18 injured players.

Van Zyl said: "There were fewer players available for us, but we are excited with the group of players that we have named for what will be a spicy derby."

Fly-half Harri Wilde, who is on loan at Ospreys from Cardiff, is named on the home replacements bench.

Ospreys flanker Harri Deaves has been ruled out for eight weeks following a knee injury he sustained in the 31-14 victory against Dragons.

Australia centre Lalakai Foketi misses out through illness and Wallabies wing Marika Koroibete was close to being in contention but will return from a rib injury after the November break.

articles.title: URC team news: Ulster's James Hume and Rob Herring return against the Stormers
articles.summary: James Hume and Rob Herring will both make their first appearances of the season when Ulster face the Stormers in the United Rugby Championship on Saturday.
articles.body:
James Hume and Rob Herring will both make their first appearances of the season when Ulster face the Stormers in the United Rugby Championship on Saturday.

Richie Murphy's side will be looking to secure a first league win of the campaign in Cape Town (12:45 GMT) having lost two and drawn two of their first four games in the competition.

With those in Andy Farrell's squad for four Nations Championship games next month already in international camp, Murphy is without eight players who were involved in last week's defeat by the Bulls, while Robert Baloucoune is also unavailable.

He is boosted, however, by the returns of centre Hume and hooker Herring, with both seeing their first action since the end of last season after injuries.

Flanker David McCann captains the selection that sees former Stormers forward Juarno Augustus start at number eight.

Ulster: McIlroy; Lowry, Hume, Carson, Ward; Murphy, Devine; O'Sullivan, Herring, Knox, Donnell, Snyman, Izuchukwu, McCann (capt), Augustus.

Replacements: Walker, McAllister, Wilson, Sheridan, Moloney, McKee, Flannery, Mullins.

Different derby day selection for Leinster

After beating Munster in Dublin last week, Leinster face a second interpro in six days as they travel to Connacht on Friday night (19:45 GMT).

The team, however, will be almost entirely different with fly-half Joey Carbery the only player who started in the Aviva Stadium last Saturday to go again at the Dexcom.

Leo Cullen has selected a whole new pack with Max Deegan coming in to captain the side from the back row.

Experienced wing Jordan Larmour will make his return from injury in the number 11 jersey, while centre Connor Fahy makes his debut.

Should he be called upon from the bench, prop Alex Mullan will also make his provincial bow.

Hosts Connacht have similarly rung the changes, making 12 alterations from their comfortable win over Zebre last week.

With eight players away on international duty, skipper Paul Boyle, prop Finlay Bealham and centre Cathal Forde are the only starters retained.

Connacht: Ioane; Bolton, Devine, Forde, Ryan; Naughton, Blade; Van Wyk, Heffernan, Bealham, Murphy, O'Connor, O'Brien, Connors, Boyle (capt).

Replacements: Victory, Cahir, Barrett, Murray, Hurley-Langton, Reilly, Treacy, Gilbert.

Leinster: Lawlor; Kenny, Fahy, Tector, Larmour; Carbery, Gunne; Usanov, McCarthy, N Smyth, Deeny, Spicer, Deegan (capt), Penny, Culhane.

Replacements: S Smyth, Dooley, Mullan, O'Tighearnaigh, Soroka, Foley, Gabriel, Mangan

Russell set for Munster debut against Sharks

Munster are the province least impacted by international call-ups with only forward Tadhg Beirne and scrum-half Craig Casey required by Farrell for the upcoming fixtures.

For Saturday's hosting of the Sharks [17:30 GMT], head coach Clayton McMillan still makes seven changes.

Former Leinster winger Rob Russell will make his Munster debut in place of the injured Shane Daly, while there is also a first provincial start for centre Gordon Wood.

Ben O'Donovan replaces Casey at scrum-half and there is also a change at 10 where the experienced JJ Hanrahan comes in for Charlie O'Shea.

Edwin Edogbo and Lee Barron are both primed for first outings of the season off the bench.

Munster: O'Connor; McCarthy, Wood, Nankivell, Russell; Hanrahan, O'Donovan; J Wycherly, Van der Merwe, Brookes; O'Connell, F Wycherly, S Edogbo, O'Donoghue (capt), Gleeson.

Replacements: Barron, Loughman, Ala'alatoa, E Edogbo, Coombes, O'Riordan, O'Shea, Kendellen.

articles.title: Kieran Hardy: Ospreys and Wales scrum-half faces World Cup fitness race
articles.summary: Wales scrum-half Kieran Hardy faces a race to be fit for next year's World Cup in Australia.
articles.body:
Wales scrum-half Kieran Hardy faces a race to be fit for next year's World Cup in Australia.

Hardy, 30, has had surgery this week after suffering a serious knee injury in the United Rugby Championship (URC) victory against Dragons at Rodney Parade .

Ospreys head coach Mark Jones has confirmed Hardy will miss the rest of the season but hopes he can be fit in time for the World Cup which starts in October 2027.

"It is a serious knee injury which has needed surgery, which tells you its extent," said Jones.

"It was a major ligament of the knee and he has got some other bits and pieces that needed rectifying as well.

"We are definitely not going to see him this season, we just hope he has a good rehabilitation, there are no kinks in the road and everything goes to plan.

"We will be crossing everything that he is around for the start of the next season and his availability with the World Cup on the horizon."

Hardy has been a regular Wales deputy for Tomos Williams, while Ospreys team-mate Reuben Morgan-Williams and the uncapped Dragons number nine Che Hope have also been named in Steve Tandy's side for the Nations Championship in November.

Wales deputy helps Ospreys make themselves at home

Where are Wales internationals really made?

Davies urged to reverse retirement for World Cup

Hardy has never played a World Cup game but was called up to the squad in the tournament in France as injury cover in 2023.

"That will be his target but you have to go with the speed the body lets you," said Jones.

"You have to have goals when you are out for a lengthy period and what better target than playing for your country at a World Cup.

"That is an awesome goal that will keep him on track. He is a great professional and he will apply himself.

"It is a huge carrot, and until somebody tells him that is not achievable, that is what he will be going for."

images.caption: Image caption, Kieran Hardy joined Ospreys from Scarlets

articles.title: Leicester Tigers: Captain Ollie Chessum signs new multi-year deal
articles.summary: Leicester Tigers captain Ollie Chessum has signed a new multi-year deal to stay at Welford Road.
articles.body:
Leicester Tigers captain Ollie Chessum has signed a new multi-year deal to stay at Welford Road.

The 26-year-old has made 88 appearances since graduating from the Tigers academy and was named club captain ahead of the 2025/26 season. He was also part of the side that won the 2022 Premiership title .

The new two-year deal comes less than a week after fellow England international Jack van Poortvliet committed his future to Leicester.

Leicester head coach Geoff Parling said: "Those young lads who have come through the academy have been developed here; they are hungry for the team to do well.

"The fans can identify themselves in them because they see a local player playing, which is really important, and they are quality players as well.

"Ollie has really developed as a captain; he's really pushing on, he's a great driver of what we do, and he's well supported from other players.

"I'd heard some good stuff about him before I arrived here but wanted to make my own mind up.

"In the first few weeks around training, I could see how he was and his desire to get better, which actually aligned with some of my bits of thinking and how we perform and how we train, which was really important.

"He's got some characteristics that I really wanted in a skipper."

Post-match round-ups and analysis on all things Tigers

images.caption: Image caption, Ollie Chessum led Leicester to a second-half comeback over Northampton Saints on Saturday

articles.title: Tadhg Furlong: Ireland prop cleared of groin grab by disciplinary committee
articles.summary: Ireland's Tadhg Furlong is cleared by a disciplinary committee of grabbing Gavin Coombes in the groin during Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster.
articles.body:
Ireland's Tadhg Furlong has been cleared by a disciplinary committee of grabbing Gavin Coombes in the groin during Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster.

Munster back row Coombes raised the allegation with match referee Andrew Brace in the first half of Leinster's 24-18 win at Aviva Stadium, but television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find conclusive video evidence.

However, three-time British and Irish Lions tourist Furlong was subsequently cited over an act of foul play under Law 9.27, which says "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals".

The disciplinary panel, comprised of Simon Thomas (Wales), Attie Heyns (South Africa) and Pamela Woodman (Scotland) met on Thursday and "unanimously concluded the citing complaint against the player should be dismissed, on the basis that he did not commit an act of foul play contrary to Law 9.27".

While they dismissed the complaint, the disciplinary committee concluded Coombes had given "an honest account of his recollection of events surrounding the incident".

Having avoided a sanction, Furlong, 33, will be available for selection for Ireland's Nations Championship home matches against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa and the finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

images.caption: Image caption, Tadhg Furlong is now cleared to play in Ireland's Nations Championship games next month
